questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/9a448574651a74ef7180549827e05ee2d790cd9fa89c6c85adf08d8444ceaadf.png)

The graph above shows $y=k({10}^{x})+c.$ Determine the values of $k$ and $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k({10}^{x})+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-3,$ so $c=-3.$

Therefore, our function takes the form

$$
y=k({10}^{x})-3.
$$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,1),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=1$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k({10}^{x})-3 \\ 1 & =k({10}^{0})-3 \\ 1 & =k(1)-3 \\ 1 & =k-3 \\ 4 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curve is $y=4({10}^{x})-3.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying the Shift and Stretch Applied to an Exponential Growth Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
The graph below shows $y=k(6^{x})+c.$ Determine the values of $k$ and $c$ and find the equation of the curve.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/deb7e20658882229a3653f4058c787bf2a5c4a26c5f2982406a2dba34c2d5846.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k(6^{x})+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=4$, so $c=4.$

Therefore, our function takes the form

$$
y=k(6^{x})+4.
$$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,6),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=6$ into the function and solve for $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k({6}^{x})+4 \\ 6 & =k({6}^{0})+4 \\ 6 & =k(1)+4 \\ 6 & =k+4 \\ 2 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curve is $y=2(6^{x})+4.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Adding a value to $y=2^x$ will **translate** (shift) the exponential function up or down the $y$-axis. 

For instance, adding $3$ to $y=2^x$ will move each point on the exponential function $3$ units up.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/c89fd5fdcdc3773143a5f14ecb20f5bd2917bce20ece18a7dc70631bf358a0e8.png)

Note the following points:

1\. The $y$-intercept $(0,1)$ has moved up $3$ units to the point $(0,4).$

2\. The horizontal asymptote $y=0$ has moved up $3$ units to $y=3.$

As a second example, let's consider the function $y=2^x-3.$ In this case, the graph of $y=2^x$ is shifted *down* by $3$ units.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/84987b3e9138a2e7e8afe70a7aa28a1cd81e081033aa2a766773e63cb8f41da5.png)

tutorials.name: Combining Vertical Shift and Vertical Stretch
tutorials.problem:
When an exponential growth function is vertically shifted *and* stretched, we apply the stretch first and the shift second.

For example, to plot the function $y=2(4^x)+3,$ we start by plotting the graph of $y=2(4^x).$ Stretching $y=4^x$ by a factor of $2$ moves the $y$-intercept from $(0,1)$ to $(0,2),$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/5d6bdd7aa3290567fc6a64747ea605970fcb1d0f05ba06907134e7fc0a3e290b.png)

Then, to plot the graph of $y=2(4^x)+3,$ we take the graph of $y=2(4^x)$ and shift it $3$ units up. The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,2)$ to $(0,5),$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/191a51b0b4b7da7c6744240f36786d55b8b525356b8d0300750fb48af5a2f06a.png)
tutorials.title: Combining Vertical Shift and Vertical Stretch
tutorials.content:
When an exponential growth function is vertically shifted *and* stretched, we apply the stretch first and the shift second.

For example, to plot the function $y=2(4^x)+3,$ we start by plotting the graph of $y=2(4^x).$ Stretching $y=4^x$ by a factor of $2$ moves the $y$-intercept from $(0,1)$ to $(0,2),$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/5d6bdd7aa3290567fc6a64747ea605970fcb1d0f05ba06907134e7fc0a3e290b.png)

Then, to plot the graph of $y=2(4^x)+3,$ we take the graph of $y=2(4^x)$ and shift it $3$ units up. The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,2)$ to $(0,5),$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14220062/assets/191a51b0b4b7da7c6744240f36786d55b8b525356b8d0300750fb48af5a2f06a.png)
